prompt.context: The CEO of Chemicals Inc., a leading chemicals company with a long history of innovative products and application technologies has contacted you for assistance. In the past couple of years, the company's bottom-line profitability has slowly eroded to the point where EBITDA is hovering barely above 0, even though the company's overall sales growth is outpacing industry averages. Magnifying these financial problems are the reports he is receiving from his business unit leaders which are that revenues and volumes are up and profitability has never been higher.
prompt.question: The CEO looks at you across the table and asks, 'What do I do?'

clarifying_info.q: Tell me about the firm's product portfolio.
clarifying_info.a: Many different kinds of chemicals products, sold to many different kinds of customers (large, small), in many different kinds of industries (automotive, medical, consumer products), all around the globe.

The company is organized geographically and by the underlying technologies that drive products, not necessarily by product line. Definition of product line is technology-application (think industry)-geography, e.g. Chemical A – Automotive – USA.

clarifying_info.q: What industries are customers of the firm's products?
clarifying_info.a: Automotive, Medical, Consumer Products (packaging), Manufacturing, Electronics, Drilling.

clarifying_info.q: How does the firm view the world in terms of regions?
clarifying_info.a: North America, South America, Europe, Pacific.

clarifying_info.q: Who are their competitors? What does the competitive landscape look like?
clarifying_info.a: Major competitors include large multi-national corporations as well as small, local, specialized firms with a single product. Some of these firms actually purchase our client's products and rework them and sell to the end customer.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs the company is incurring?
clarifying_info.a: Revenues last year were $2Bn. The COGS is variable, about 25%, but all companies in this industry are dealing with fluctuating feedstock prices. SG&A expense is 30% of revenue and beyond the industry benchmark. Other costs are inline with industry norms.

exhibits.title: Product Line Contribution Margins
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing contribution margins (in $/kg) across 15 product lines. Each bar represents a distinct product line. The bars are color-coded by business unit: Technology A, Technology B, and Technology C. The y-axis ranges from 0 to approximately 250 $/kg.
exhibits.data: Y-axis: Contribution Margins ($/kg), scale 0–250; 15 bars total; colors distinguish Technology A, Technology B, and Technology C product lines; wide dispersion of margin levels across the portfolio.

framework: Identify cost problem: Sales and volumes are up but EBITDA near zero — focus on COGS and SG&A relative to revenue growth
Diagnose cost allocation mismatch: Business units report profitability gains while the company overall is losing — suggests shared costs are not allocated properly
Analyze product/service mix: Examine 15 product lines (3 technologies × 5 industries) for contribution margin variation — determine which are specialty vs. commodity
Assess customer needs by segment: Understand what each industry customer actually values and is willing to pay for
Evaluate pricing alignment: Determine whether the company is undercharging for high-value products and services
Develop reorganization recommendation: Realign business units and service model based on margin profile

questions.prompt: The company has 3 chemical technologies sold into 5 industries. How many product lines does that yield, and what does Exhibit 1 tell you?
questions.guidance: 3 technologies × 5 industries = 15 product lines. Exhibit 1 shows wide dispersion in contribution margins across those 15 lines — indicating significant commoditization of many lines. Business units (Technology A, B, C) are spread across the margin continuum, meaning no single BU cleanly owns the high-margin or low-margin segment. The key insight is that product lines should be realigned by margin profile (specialty vs. commodity), not by technology.

math.setup: Number of product lines = Number of technologies × Number of industries
steps: 3 technologies (A, B, C) × 5 industries (Automotive, Medical, Consumer Products, Electronics, Drilling) = 15 product lines

questions.prompt: Given revenues of $2Bn, COGS of 25%, and SG&A of 30%, what is the approximate EBITDA margin and dollar EBITDA? Why is SG&A a problem?
questions.guidance: COGS + SG&A alone = 55% of revenue, leaving only ~45% for other costs, depreciation, and profit. Since EBITDA is barely above 0, total costs must be approaching ~100% of revenue. The SG&A at 30% is explicitly cited as 'beyond the industry benchmark,' meaning the company is overspending on selling, general and administrative costs relative to peers — this is the primary cost lever to address.

math.setup: Revenue = $2Bn; COGS = 25% of revenue; SG&A = 30% of revenue
steps: Remaining for other costs and EBITDA = $2Bn − $1.1Bn = $900M
Since EBITDA ≈ 0, other costs (manufacturing overhead, R&D, etc.) consume nearly the remaining $900M
math.answer: SG&A alone is $600M and above industry benchmark; combined with COGS the company has very little room for profit before other costs are applied.

questions.prompt: Why might business units report profitability gains while the overall company shows near-zero EBITDA?
questions.guidance: The disconnect arises from cost allocation. Shared services (technical support, logistics, customer service, application development, financing terms) are provided to ALL product lines equally but costs may not be allocated back to the individual product lines or business units that consume them. High-cost-to-serve commodity customers are effectively subsidized by the system. Business units measure only their direct revenues and directly allocated costs, missing the shared service overhead that is dragging down total EBITDA.

questions.prompt: What do the different customer industries actually need and value? Which are price-sensitive vs. willing to pay for service?
questions.guidance: Automotive: Very price-conscious for most parts, except safety applications and consumer-touch interior components. Consumer Goods/Packaging: Very cost-conscious, cannot pass costs on (e.g. plastic cups, plates, wrap). Electronics: Generally need inexpensive products but willing to pay more for small lot sizes and specialized custom technical support. Medical: Very specialized applications (e.g. lenses), can pass costs along to customers — high willingness to pay. Drilling: Huge costs from broken parts, so want the best products available — high willingness to pay for quality. Insight: Medical and Drilling are natural 'Specialty' segments; Consumer Goods and most of Automotive are natural 'Commodity' segments; Electronics is mixed.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional changes might you consider for an organization facing increased commoditization of its product lines? How might the organization reduce volatility in raw materials / COGS?

categories.name: Product & Portfolio Strategy
ideas: Rationalize the product portfolio — exit the lowest-margin commodity lines where the firm has no competitive advantage
Invest in R&D to continuously develop new specialty/high-margin products before existing ones commoditize
Develop industry-specific product bundles that combine commodity and specialty offerings to improve overall margin mix

categories.name: Pricing & Go-to-Market
ideas: Introduce tiered or a la carte pricing for services (small batch, custom logistics, technical support) rather than bundling all services free
Implement value-based pricing for specialty segments (Medical, Drilling) where customers have high willingness to pay
Use cost-plus or competitive pricing for commodity segments to remain competitive without over-investing

categories.name: Cost Structure & Operations
ideas: Hedge raw material / feedstock prices using futures contracts or long-term supplier agreements to reduce COGS volatility
Develop strategic supplier partnerships or vertical integration for critical feedstocks
Implement lean manufacturing and process optimization to lower per-unit production costs in commodity lines
Outsource or automate low-complexity commodity fulfillment to reduce SG&A

categories.name: Organizational Design
ideas: Create dedicated industry-specific sales teams that span technology business units to improve customer focus
Establish clear ownership and accountability for shared service costs with service-level agreements between BUs and shared functions
Consider divesting one of the business units to focus capital and management attention

categories.name: Customer & Channel Strategy
ideas: Increase partnerships and long-term contracts with specialty customers to secure volume in high-margin segments
Selectively reduce service levels for commodity customers to right-size cost-to-serve
Explore channel partners or distributors for commodity products to reduce direct SG&A

recommendation: Reorganize the company into two business units: Specialty and Commodity, aligned by contribution margin profile rather than technology

The Specialty business unit should continue to provide a high level of customized service (small batches, custom logistics, application development support, favorable financing terms) to high-margin customers such as Medical and Drilling

The Commodity business unit should adopt a lower-cost service model with IT-enabled self-service tools, a la carte service agreements, and less favorable terms and conditions — targeting Automotive (standard parts) and Consumer Goods segments

Develop a shared service model that embeds business unit-specialized functions into each BU and retains only general functions (legal, HR, facilities) at corporate core; each shared service function should have a single leader accountable for cost and responsible for negotiating service agreements with BU leaders to ensure appropriate allocation
risks: Appropriate and ongoing assignment of product lines to Specialty vs. Commodity BUs — lines may shift over time as markets evolve
Business units do not own manufacturing and supply chain, so these remain holders of unallocated cost with little incentive to optimize
Reducing personal service levels for commodity customers may make the firm less competitive and erode top-line revenues and volumes in those segments
next_steps: Study manufacturing and supply chain to allocate those costs to business units where practical
Increase partnerships with Specialty Chemicals customers to grow volume in high-margin business
Consider outsourcing or selling one of the business units to sharpen strategic focus, or develop a portfolio strategy with major customers via industry-specific sales teams that span business units
